Integrated model of spaceflight stress on immune dysfunction

The spaceflight exposome collectively perturbs immune cell biology. Spaceflight fosters resilient microbes, heightening immune vulnerability. Chronic physiological stress raises cortisol, binding glucocorticoid receptors, suppressing NF-κB-mediated inflammation, and also facilitating lymphocyte apoptosis. Cosmic radiation increases the levels of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and RNS), damaging cellular structures, activating inflammatory pathways, and also potentially enabling immune cell apoptosis. Microgravity induces alterations in GPCR expression in PBMCs, which may modulate PKA and Rho family GTPase activity, regulates ion channel activation and integrins, perturbing cytoskeleton organization. Cytoskeleton remodelling affects nuclear and cell shape likely via the LINC complex. Changes in the cytoskeleton also disrupts mitochondrial function. Altered GPCR activity, especially in T cells, potentially modulates calcium levels, worsening mitochondrial health. Altered actin remodelling and microgravity regulate nuclear receptor levels across PBMCs and reduce PKC translocation to influence inflammation, metabolism and activation. Cytoskeleton dynamics are also key in RLR, and potentially TLR mediated antiviral pathways, where microgravity deregulates RIG-I and TRIM25, which ubiquitinates RIG-I in innate immune cells. This change impedes interaction with MAVS, blocking downstream antiviral signalling and IFN expression. Spaceflight stressors, including microgravity, also regulate chromosome conformation, including epigenetic docking sites for transcription factors, affecting gene expression, as shown in T lymphocytes. For instance, FOXP3 shows increased chromatin docking in regulatory T (Treg cells) after spaceflight.Other space stressors, including cosmic radiation, further impair mitochondria function, prompting caspase-3 activation and apoptosis. At the same time, ROS released from damaged mitochondria upregulate the HIF-1 pathway, affecting immune metabolism and inflammation. ROS coupled with other damaged cellular components further incite low-grade basal inflammation potentially through inflammasomes or nucleic acid-sensing mechanisms. Consistently, within the nucleus, cosmic radiation inflicts telomere stress and DNA damage, prompting cells to upregulate DNA repair proteins. However, microgravity impairs DNA damage responses, causing immune cells to accumulate DNA damage, predisposing them to apoptosis, further inflammatory changes or potentially senescence. Altogether, the space stressors elevate inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, reduce IFN signalling, suppress adaptive immune responses and proliferation to stimulation, and reduce innate cell phagocytosis and antigen presentation. These changes, coupled to changes in chromatin conformation, contribute to viral reactivation. Changes in microRNA (miRNA) and long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) levels have been documented in cells in space, and likely contribute to these processes.Solid lines are published mechanistic connections, while dotted lines are hypothetical mechanistic connections for spaceflight stressors. Black arrows represent pathways and phenotypes found in PBMCs (proposed or observed). Red arrows specifically denote pathways and phenotypes found in innate immune cells, blue arrows specifically denote pathways and phenotypes described in adaptive immune cells. IFN, interferon; miRNA, micro-RNA; lncRNA, long-non-coding RNA. ROS, Reactive oxygen species; RNS, reactive nitrogen species; LINC, linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton; RLR, retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors; TRIM25, tripartite motif containing 25; HIF-1, hypoxia-inducible factor 1; MAVS, Mitochondrial antiviral signalling protein; GPCR, G protein-coupled receptor; PKC, Protein Kinase C; PKA, Protein Kinase A
